Thanks for the quick SIG turnaround so far. Our security team needs a few architecture clarifications and evidence to complete the questionnaire for our procurement cycle:

1) Connectivity modes — you referenced both VPC peering (Dedicated) and PrivateLink/private endpoints (Hosted Private). For a hosted PrivateLink integration, can you confirm whether Fintech Co needs a VPC peering relationship with Redwood, or if AWS PrivateLink is sufficient to keep traffic entirely within our VPC?

2) Egress/source IPs — our firewall team requires a stable list of source IPs (or CIDR blocks) for any outgoing connections originating from Redwood infrastructure to our services during the onboarding tests and daily operation. Do you provide committed/stable egress ranges we can allowlist? If ranges change, what is the notification window?

3) Evidence artifacts — please provide a network diagram, an IP allowlist (CSV), and any standard runbook we can use to perform a connectivity test. If you have a signed attestation or SOC/SIG mappings relevant to network controls, please attach.

Hi Claire — thanks for the clear list. High level answers first, details and artifacts below and attached.

Summary answers:
- PrivateLink (AWS Network Load Balancer backed endpoint service / interface endpoints) is supported and does NOT require VPC peering for hosted Private deployments; it keeps traffic within AWS private networking between your VPC and our service endpoint.
- For hosted (non-dedicated) traffic over the public internet we publish stable NAT egress ranges you can allowlist. For PrivateLink traffic, your VPC initiates the connection to our service endpoint so there are no Redwood-originated public egress IPs to allowlist.
- For Dedicated (customer-dedicated GPU fleet) customers that want L2/L3 network connectivity we support VPC peering or transit setup, but peering is optional and typically used for high-throughput, low-latency private networks.

Attachments included (PDF/CSV):
- redwood_network_diagram_v2.pdf  (high-level topology, shows Hosted/Private/Dedicated flows)
- redwood_egress_ips_20261218.csv (stable NAT egress CIDRs for hosted API egress)
- privatelink_integration_guide.pdf (how to create interface endpoints and confirm route tables/security groups)

Key details you can give to your network team:
- Hosted API (public): allow outbound HTTPS to these source NAT CIDRs (we use AWS-managed NAT EIPs across regions). Current egress CIDRs (US regions): 34.210.12.0/22, 52.24.128.0/22, 3.21.56.0/23. These are stable ranges; we issue a 30-day notice for planned changes and will publish changes to the HubSpot ticket and the Drive link below.
- PrivateLink/Interface Endpoint: No Redwood public egress IPs. You will create an AWS Interface Endpoint (com.amazonaws.vpce) that connects to our endpoint service in the same region. Configure security groups to allow the customer subnets to reach the endpoint on 443.
- Dedicated (private VPC): we support VPC Peering or AWS Transit Gateway. If you choose peering, we'll exchange account/region/peer CIDRs and provide peering request templates.

Runbook excerpt (attach and summarize):
- Create Interface Endpoint in your VPC and enable private DNS (if you want hostname resolution to resolve to the ENI).
- Update client SGs to permit outbound to the endpoint ENI on TCP/443.
- From your test host run: curl -v https://api.redwood.com/healthcheck and validate response headers include x-rw-region.

If you need a signed attestation for egress ranges and architecture, I can escalate for a short attestation PDF.

I'll follow up with an internal ops message to prepare the signed attestation and formal CSV.

Best,
Marcus Lin
Sr. Solutions Engineer, Network Integrations
Redwood Inference
